Phosphine-catalyzed sequential (2+3)/(2+4)
annulation of c-vinyl allenoates: access to the
synthesis of chromeno[4,3- b]pyrroles†‡
Xiaohu Li and You Huang
 *
A phosphine-catalyzed cascade (2+3)/(2+4) cyclization reaction of
c-vinyl allenoates with aldimine esters has been developed to
provide a series of chromeno[4,3- b]pyrrole derivatives that contain
three contiguous stereogenic centers. The method gives a good
yield, excellent chemoselectivity and diastereoselectivity under
mild conditions.
Chromeno[4,3-b]pyrrole and its structural analogues are ubiqui-
tous moieties in natural products, biologically active products and
pharmaceuticals (Fig. 1). For instance, lamellarins,1 al a r g ef a m i l y
of marine alkaloids isolated from diverse marine ascidians and
sponges, have been identified as lead compounds for the inhibi-
tion of topoisomerase I and HIV-1 integrase. Martinelline or
martinellic acid alkaloids
2 with a similar structural moiety of
chromeno[4,3-b]pyrrole could act as a bradykinin receptor antago-
nist and have antibacterial activity. Chromeno[4,3-b]pyrrole deri-
vatives also have promising utilities in medicinal chemistry, such
as the treatment of Parkinson’s disease, impulsive disorders and
inflammation.
3
Given their promising biological activities, chromeno-
[4,3-b]pyrrole frameworks have drawn considerable attention
from both organic and medicinal chemists. To date, successful
methodologies have been developed and the most accessible
routes to chromeno[4,3- b]pyrrole skeletons involve 1,3-dipolar
cycloaddition (1,3-DC) between alkenes and azomethine ylides
as a key step.
4 In addition, organo-catalyzed, metal-free strategies
have also completed the construction of chromeno[4,3- b]pyrrole
frameworks in recent years. 5 Because of their remarkable
potential pharmaceutical value, atom-economic, environment-
friendly, and more eﬃcient methods for the construction of the
chromeno[4,3-b]pyrrole moiety with excellent yields and diaster-
eoselectivity are still highly desired.
In 1995, the first nucleophilic phosphine-catalyzed annulation
reaction of allenoates was reported by Lu.
6a The seminal eﬃcient
methods for rapid construction of the five-membered carbocyclic
moiety have been used in the total synthesis of natural products
successfully.
6b,c Since then, domino annulation reactions of unsub-
stituted allenoates catalyzed by nucleophilic phosphines have been
one of the most eﬃcient strategies for the rapid construction of
cyclic products.7 When there are diﬀerent substituents at diﬀerent
sites in allenoates, they will exhibit diverse reactivity and could
construct bicyclic compounds eﬃciently. For example, Huang’s
group
8 and other groups 9 realized phosphine-catalyzed bicyclic
annulation reactions usingg-methyl or g-benzyl allenoates, respec-
tively. Moreover, the groups of Tong, 10 Shi11 and Zhou 5e have
independently carried out interesting studies on allenoates with a
leaving group such as an acetoxyl group at the b0 or d-position to
construct bicyclic skeletons. R ecently, our group has designed
d-sulfonamido-allenoates and developed sequential (3+3)/(3+3)
bicyclic annulation reactions using these new substituted alleno-
ates successfully.12
The reactivity of substituted allenoates inspired us to install
a g-vinyl group on allenoates to extend the p-system and
increase versatile reactivity. Fortunately, we first reported
phosphine-catalyzed remote 1,7-addition for synthesis of diene
carboxylates using g-vinyl allenoates. 13 We assume that g-vinyl
allenoates could undergo sequential annulation reactions
because of multiple reactive sites. In 2019, our group reported

using g-vinyl allenoates (eqn (1) in Scheme 1), in which they
participated in reactions as a threefold preelectrophile. 14 Later,
with our nuanced work on g-vinyl allenoates, we successfully
developed phosphine-catalyzed (3+2)/(3+2) annulation reac-
tions using allenoates as a new reaction model to construct
highly crowded fused carbocycles
15 (eqn (2) in Scheme 1). To
investigate new reactive possibilities of g-vinyl allenoates,
herein, we report a phosphine-catalyzed reaction using aldi-
mine esters as partners with three disparate reactive sites to
develop new domino processes. However, several problematic
issues need to be overcome: (1) chemoselectivity control of
aldimine esters with one more nucleophile site; (2) regioselec-
tivity control on reaction-sites of g-vinyl allenoates, such as the
electrophilic b position, and electrophilic g or e positions after
nucleophilic phosphine addition forming a zwitterion; (3)
diﬃcult diastereoselectivity control of annulation products.
Initially, we started the investigation by employing aldimine
ester ( 1a) and g-vinyl allenoate ( 2a) as model substrates to
validate the feasibility of our hypothesis. Gratifyingly, the
desired product 3aa in 50% yield was obtained catalyzed by
PPh
3 (30 mol%) in toluene at 25 1C (see Table S1, entry 1, ESI †),
and the structure and relative configuration of 3aa was con-
firmed by X-ray crystallographic analysis. After a systematic
screening of organophosphine catalysts was conducted, weakly
nucleophilic phosphines (see Table S1, entries 1 and 2, ESI †)
gave better results than strongly nucleophilic phosphines (see
Table S1, entries 3–6, ESI †). To further improve the yield,
additives were surveyed using ( p-FC
6H4)3P as the catalyst. These
results revealed that weak acids had a positive impact and
PhCOOH (100 mol%) was proved to be the best choice, afford-
ing 3aa in 82% yield with excellent diastereoselectivity ratio
(420 : 1). Moreover, various solvents were investigated and the
process gave the best outcome when using toluene as the
solvent. Finally, using ( p-FC
6H4)3P (30 mol%) as the catalyst,
and PhCOOH (100 mol%) as the additive and conducting the
reaction in toluene at 25 1C for 2 hours were identified as
optimal reaction conditions.
With the optimized reaction conditions in hand, the sub-
strate scope and limitations of the reaction were surveyed and
the results are shown in Table 1. The aldimine esters ( 1b–1h)
bearing an electron-donating group or a halide as well as the
ester-containing alkyl group (R 1 = 4-CH 2CO2Me) at the para
position of the phenol ring reacted smoothly and gave the
corresponding products in good yields with excellent diaster-
eoselectivity ( 3ba–3ha in Table 1). Similarly, the reaction of an
aldimine ester bearing a monosubstituted group at the ortho
and meta positions of the phenol ring also proceeded well and
gave acceptable yields ( 3ia–3na in Table 1). The aldimine ester
bearing an aromatic group at the para position of the phenol
ring worked well and gave the expected compound 3oa in 77%
yield. It is worth noting that aldimine esters with a disubsiti-
tuted aromatic group went smoothly without an apparent
decline in the yield ( 3pa and 3qa). The aldimine ester bearing
a naphthyl group proceeded very well, giving the product 3ra in
96% yield. Furthermore, the reactivity of substrate aldimine
esters with a strong electron-withdrawing group on the benzene
ring was investigated. Most of these substrates could react
smoothly in spite of the obvious electronic effects. Notably,
the aldimine esters bearing –CO
2Me or –CF 3 at the para posi-
tion of the phenol ring led to moderate yields 69% and 54%,

respectively ( 3sa and 3ta in Table 1). In comparison, the
reaction gave 80% ( 3ua in Table 1) yield when the –CO 2Me
group was at the meta position of the phenol ring. Because of
strong electron-deficient trisubstituted boron atoms, the sub-
strate 1v gave a relatively low yield under the optimized reaction
conditions. Interestingly, it could rise to 41% when the reaction
was carried out with buffer (PhCOONa/PhCOOH, 1 equiv./
1 equiv.). This may be due to the coordination effect of
PhCOONa on boron, which reduces the electron deficiency of
the boron atom and enhances the nucleophilicity of phenolic
hydroxyl. However, with a nitro group at the para position of the
phenol ring, the expected product could not be obtained ( 3wa).
Furthermore, the effect of the ester substituent at the g-vinyl
allenoate (2) and malonate moiety was studied, and the desired
products were obtained in moderate to good yields ( 3xa, 3ya,
3ab, 3ac, and 3ad).
To validate the practicality of this tandem annulation reac-
tion, gram-scale experiments were carried out using 1a (1.0 g,
3.6 mmol) and 1x (1.0 g, 4.0 mmol), and obtained the corres-
ponding products 3aa (1.4 g, 65% yield) and 3xa (1.14 g, 71%),
respectively (Scheme 2a). To illustrate the potential utility of
this new methodology, the post-functionalization of product
3xa was carried out (Scheme 2b). The carbon–carbon double
bond on the side chain of 3xa was reduced by heterogeneous
catalytic hydrogenation; meanwhile, the benzyl group was
removed at the same time, followed by addition of catalytic
amounts of sulfuric acid to afford the Fisher esterification
product 4 in 96% yield in one pot. Next, 4 was decarboxylated
by the Krapcho protocol
16 to give 5 in 35% yield.
Following the substrate scope evaluation, control experi-
ments were carried out to gain insight into the mechanism of
the reaction. Under the standard conditions, no corresponding
product was obtained when allenoate 2a reacted with ethyl
(E)-2-[(2-hydroxybenzylidene)amino]acetate 6, suggesting that
the malonate moiety is necessary to trigger the reaction
(eqn (1) in Scheme 3). Replacement of the hydroxyl group with
an amido group or 4-methyl benzenesulfonamido group
(p-TsNH) did not give the desired product, revealing that the
hydroxyl group is essential (eqn (2) in Scheme 3). In addition,
changing the hydroxyl group to a methoxy group, no new
product was obtained (eqn (3) in Scheme 3). When 10 equiv.
of D
2O was added to the reaction mixture under standard
conditions, we obtained the deuterated product d-3aa in 58%
yield. 1H NMR analysis showed remarkable H/D exchange at the
C9, C15, and C16 positions.
Based on the results of control and deuterium-labeling
experiments, the ortho hydroxyl group of the benzene ring
was essential, and it might be important to increase the
electrophilic reactivity of the imine via an intramolecular
hydrogen bond. A putative mechanism of the cascade annula-
tion reaction is illustrated in Fig. 2. First, the nucleophilic
addition of ( p-FC
6H4)3P to allenoate 2a followed by being
protonated by PhCOOH led to the Michael acceptor II. Remote
1,7-addition13 of the reactive enolate I to the acceptor II formed
the first s-bond and generated intermediate III. The intermedi-
ate III could resonate to give IV, which was activated by an
intramolecular hydrogen bond and carried out intramolecular
addition of the carbon anion to vinyl phosphonium to aﬀord
intermediate V. Then after the addition of phenolate to the
electron deficient double bond, the second cyclization was
done via intramolecular formal (2+4) cycloaddition. Finally,

the elimination of the phosphine catalyst yielded product 3aa,
and regenerated the phosphine catalyst ( p-FC6H4)3P, which
continued the next catalytic cycle.
It should be noted that the naphthyl-substituted substrate
1ra gave the target product in almost quantitative yield ( 3ra in
Table 1). We assumed that there was another mechanism
(bottom in Fig. 2). The resonated intermediate IV-1ra after
remote 1,7-addition went through [1,5] H-shift and dearomati-
zation to obtain the highly active o-quinone methide inter-
mediate VIII, which then carried out the subsequent reaction to
give the target compound 3ra. A similar mechanism was also
proposed by many groups for addition reactions with o-quinone
methide as a key active intermediate.
17 Extension of the aro-
matic system in substrate 1ra allowed for a decreased energetic
penalty for the breaking of aromaticity in the phenyl core, and
formed the o-quinone methide intermediate eﬃciently during
the reaction, and other substrates had not these intrinsic
qualities. This may be the reason for the high yield of the
product 3ra.
In conclusion, we have developed a phosphine-catalyzed
cascade (2+3)/(2+4) annulation reaction of g-vinyl allenoates
with aldimine esters. This procedure constructs three s-bonds
and three contiguous stereogenic centers in a one-pot method
to assemble chromeno[4,3- b]pyrrole derivatives directly in good
yields with excellent chemoselectivity and diastereoselectivity
under mild conditions. Finally, control and deuterium-labeling
experiments provided deeper insight into the reaction mecha-
nism. Mechanistic studies revealed that an intramolecular
hydrogen bond is important for the reaction to run smoothly.

Phosphine-catalyzed sequential (2+3)/(2+4)
annulation of c-vinyl allenoates: access to the
synthesis of chromeno[4,3- b]pyrroles†‡
Xiaohu Li and You Huang
 *
A phosphine-catalyzed cascade (2+3)/(2+4) cyclization reaction of
c-vinyl allenoates with aldimine esters has been developed to
provide a series of chromeno[4,3- b]pyrrole derivatives that contain
three contiguous stereogenic centers. The method gives a good
yield, excellent chemoselectivity and diastereoselectivity under
mild conditions.
Chromeno[4,3-b]pyrrole and its structural analogues are ubiqui-
tous moieties in natural products, biologically active products and
pharmaceuticals (Fig. 1). For instance, lamellarins,1 al a r g ef a m i l y
of marine alkaloids isolated from diverse marine ascidians and
sponges, have been identified as lead compounds for the inhibi-
tion of topoisomerase I and HIV-1 integrase. Martinelline or
martinellic acid alkaloids
2 with a similar structural moiety of
chromeno[4,3-b]pyrrole could act as a bradykinin receptor antago-
nist and have antibacterial activity. Chromeno[4,3-b]pyrrole deri-
vatives also have promising utilities in medicinal chemistry, such
as the treatment of Parkinson’s disease, impulsive disorders and
inflammation.
3
Given their promising biological activities, chromeno-
[4,3-b]pyrrole frameworks have drawn considerable attention
from both organic and medicinal chemists. To date, successful
methodologies have been developed and the most accessible
routes to chromeno[4,3- b]pyrrole skeletons involve 1,3-dipolar
cycloaddition (1,3-DC) between alkenes and azomethine ylides
as a key step.
4 In addition, organo-catalyzed, metal-free strategies
have also completed the construction of chromeno[4,3- b]pyrrole
frameworks in recent years. 5 Because of their remarkable
potential pharmaceutical value, atom-economic, environment-
friendly, and more eﬃcient methods for the construction of the
chromeno[4,3-b]pyrrole moiety with excellent yields and diaster-
eoselectivity are still highly desired.
In 1995, the first nucleophilic phosphine-catalyzed annulation
reaction of allenoates was reported by Lu.
6a The seminal eﬃcient
methods for rapid construction of the five-membered carbocyclic
moiety have been used in the total synthesis of natural products
successfully.
6b,c Since then, domino annulation reactions of unsub-
stituted allenoates catalyzed by nucleophilic phosphines have been
one of the most eﬃcient strategies for the rapid construction of
cyclic products.7 When there are diﬀerent substituents at diﬀerent
sites in allenoates, they will exhibit diverse reactivity and could
construct bicyclic compounds eﬃciently. For example, Huang’s
group
8 and other groups 9 realized phosphine-catalyzed bicyclic
annulation reactions usingg-methyl or g-benzyl allenoates, respec-
tively. Moreover, the groups of Tong, 10 Shi11 and Zhou 5e have
independently carried out interesting studies on allenoates with a
leaving group such as an acetoxyl group at the b0 or d-position to
construct bicyclic skeletons. R ecently, our group has designed
d-sulfonamido-allenoates and developed sequential (3+3)/(3+3)
bicyclic annulation reactions using these new substituted alleno-
ates successfully.12
The reactivity of substituted allenoates inspired us to install
a g-vinyl group on allenoates to extend the p-system and
increase versatile reactivity. Fortunately, we first reported
phosphine-catalyzed remote 1,7-addition for synthesis of diene
carboxylates using g-vinyl allenoates. 13 We assume that g-vinyl
allenoates could undergo sequential annulation reactions
because of multiple reactive sites. In 2019, our group reported

participated in reactions as a threefold preelectrophile. 14 Later,
with our nuanced work on g-vinyl allenoates, we successfully
developed phosphine-catalyzed (3+2)/(3+2) annulation reac-
tions using allenoates as a new reaction model to construct
highly crowded fused carbocycles
15 (eqn (2) in Scheme 1). To
investigate new reactive possibilities of g-vinyl allenoates,
herein, we report a phosphine-catalyzed reaction using aldi-
mine esters as partners with three disparate reactive sites to
develop new domino processes. However, several problematic
issues need to be overcome: (1) chemoselectivity control of
aldimine esters with one more nucleophile site; (2) regioselec-
tivity control on reaction-sites of g-vinyl allenoates, such as the
electrophilic b position, and electrophilic g or e positions after
nucleophilic phosphine addition forming a zwitterion; (3)
diﬃcult diastereoselectivity control of annulation products.
Initially, we started the investigation by employing aldimine
ester ( 1a) and g-vinyl allenoate ( 2a) as model substrates to
validate the feasibility of our hypothesis. Gratifyingly, the
desired product 3aa in 50% yield was obtained catalyzed by
PPh
3 (30 mol%) in toluene at 25 1C (see Table S1, entry 1, ESI †),
and the structure and relative configuration of 3aa was con-
firmed by X-ray crystallographic analysis. After a systematic
screening of organophosphine catalysts was conducted, weakly
nucleophilic phosphines (see Table S1, entries 1 and 2, ESI †)
gave better results than strongly nucleophilic phosphines (see
Table S1, entries 3–6, ESI †). To further improve the yield,
additives were surveyed using ( p-FC
6H4)3P as the catalyst. These
results revealed that weak acids had a positive impact and
PhCOOH (100 mol%) was proved to be the best choice, afford-
ing 3aa in 82% yield with excellent diastereoselectivity ratio
(420 : 1). Moreover, various solvents were investigated and the
process gave the best outcome when using toluene as the
solvent. Finally, using ( p-FC
6H4)3P (30 mol%) as the catalyst,
and PhCOOH (100 mol%) as the additive and conducting the
reaction in toluene at 25 1C for 2 hours were identified as
optimal reaction conditions.
With the optimized reaction conditions in hand, the sub-
strate scope and limitations of the reaction were surveyed and
the results are shown in Table 1. The aldimine esters ( 1b–1h)
bearing an electron-donating group or a halide as well as the
ester-containing alkyl group (R 1 = 4-CH 2CO2Me) at the para
position of the phenol ring reacted smoothly and gave the
corresponding products in good yields with excellent diaster-
eoselectivity ( 3ba–3ha in Table 1). Similarly, the reaction of an
aldimine ester bearing a monosubstituted group at the ortho
and meta positions of the phenol ring also proceeded well and
gave acceptable yields ( 3ia–3na in Table 1). The aldimine ester
bearing an aromatic group at the para position of the phenol
ring worked well and gave the expected compound 3oa in 77%
yield. It is worth noting that aldimine esters with a disubsiti-
tuted aromatic group went smoothly without an apparent
decline in the yield ( 3pa and 3qa). The aldimine ester bearing
a naphthyl group proceeded very well, giving the product 3ra in
96% yield. Furthermore, the reactivity of substrate aldimine
esters with a strong electron-withdrawing group on the benzene
ring was investigated. Most of these substrates could react
smoothly in spite of the obvious electronic effects. Notably,
the aldimine esters bearing –CO
2Me or –CF 3 at the para posi-
tion of the phenol ring led to moderate yields 69% and 54%,

reaction gave 80% ( 3ua in Table 1) yield when the –CO 2Me
group was at the meta position of the phenol ring. Because of
strong electron-deficient trisubstituted boron atoms, the sub-
strate 1v gave a relatively low yield under the optimized reaction
conditions. Interestingly, it could rise to 41% when the reaction
was carried out with buffer (PhCOONa/PhCOOH, 1 equiv./
1 equiv.). This may be due to the coordination effect of
PhCOONa on boron, which reduces the electron deficiency of
the boron atom and enhances the nucleophilicity of phenolic
hydroxyl. However, with a nitro group at the para position of the
phenol ring, the expected product could not be obtained ( 3wa).
Furthermore, the effect of the ester substituent at the g-vinyl
allenoate (2) and malonate moiety was studied, and the desired
products were obtained in moderate to good yields ( 3xa, 3ya,
3ab, 3ac, and 3ad).
To validate the practicality of this tandem annulation reac-
tion, gram-scale experiments were carried out using 1a (1.0 g,
3.6 mmol) and 1x (1.0 g, 4.0 mmol), and obtained the corres-
ponding products 3aa (1.4 g, 65% yield) and 3xa (1.14 g, 71%),
respectively (Scheme 2a). To illustrate the potential utility of
this new methodology, the post-functionalization of product
3xa was carried out (Scheme 2b). The carbon–carbon double
bond on the side chain of 3xa was reduced by heterogeneous
catalytic hydrogenation; meanwhile, the benzyl group was
removed at the same time, followed by addition of catalytic
amounts of sulfuric acid to afford the Fisher esterification
product 4 in 96% yield in one pot. Next, 4 was decarboxylated
by the Krapcho protocol
16 to give 5 in 35% yield.
Following the substrate scope evaluation, control experi-
ments were carried out to gain insight into the mechanism of
the reaction. Under the standard conditions, no corresponding
product was obtained when allenoate 2a reacted with ethyl
(E)-2-[(2-hydroxybenzylidene)amino]acetate 6, suggesting that
the malonate moiety is necessary to trigger the reaction
(eqn (1) in Scheme 3). Replacement of the hydroxyl group with
an amido group or 4-methyl benzenesulfonamido group
(p-TsNH) did not give the desired product, revealing that the
hydroxyl group is essential (eqn (2) in Scheme 3). In addition,
changing the hydroxyl group to a methoxy group, no new
product was obtained (eqn (3) in Scheme 3). When 10 equiv.
of D
2O was added to the reaction mixture under standard
conditions, we obtained the deuterated product d-3aa in 58%
yield. 1H NMR analysis showed remarkable H/D exchange at the
C9, C15, and C16 positions.
Based on the results of control and deuterium-labeling
experiments, the ortho hydroxyl group of the benzene ring
was essential, and it might be important to increase the
electrophilic reactivity of the imine via an intramolecular
hydrogen bond. A putative mechanism of the cascade annula-
tion reaction is illustrated in Fig. 2. First, the nucleophilic
addition of ( p-FC
6H4)3P to allenoate 2a followed by being
protonated by PhCOOH led to the Michael acceptor II. Remote
1,7-addition13 of the reactive enolate I to the acceptor II formed
the first s-bond and generated intermediate III. The intermedi-
ate III could resonate to give IV, which was activated by an
intramolecular hydrogen bond and carried out intramolecular
addition of the carbon anion to vinyl phosphonium to aﬀord
intermediate V. Then after the addition of phenolate to the
electron deficient double bond, the second cyclization was
done via intramolecular formal (2+4) cycloaddition. Finally,

and regenerated the phosphine catalyst ( p-FC6H4)3P, which
continued the next catalytic cycle.
It should be noted that the naphthyl-substituted substrate
1ra gave the target product in almost quantitative yield ( 3ra in
Table 1). We assumed that there was another mechanism
(bottom in Fig. 2). The resonated intermediate IV-1ra after
remote 1,7-addition went through [1,5] H-shift and dearomati-
zation to obtain the highly active o-quinone methide inter-
mediate VIII, which then carried out the subsequent reaction to
give the target compound 3ra. A similar mechanism was also
proposed by many groups for addition reactions with o-quinone
methide as a key active intermediate.
17 Extension of the aro-
matic system in substrate 1ra allowed for a decreased energetic
penalty for the breaking of aromaticity in the phenyl core, and
formed the o-quinone methide intermediate eﬃciently during
the reaction, and other substrates had not these intrinsic
qualities. This may be the reason for the high yield of the
product 3ra.
In conclusion, we have developed a phosphine-catalyzed
cascade (2+3)/(2+4) annulation reaction of g-vinyl allenoates
with aldimine esters. This procedure constructs three s-bonds
and three contiguous stereogenic centers in a one-pot method
to assemble chromeno[4,3- b]pyrrole derivatives directly in good
yields with excellent chemoselectivity and diastereoselectivity
under mild conditions. Finally, control and deuterium-labeling
experiments provided deeper insight into the reaction mecha-
nism. Mechanistic studies revealed that an intramolecular
hydrogen bond is important for the reaction to run smoothly.
